Recency sampling and deterministic weighting can match expected objectives, but only with identical target contexts, negative sampling, and loss reduction. For eligible positions t=1,…,n, define p_t=exp[−λ(n−t)]/Z_n. Sampling one target with probability p_t and using its unweighted loss has expectation Σ_t p_tℓ_t. Per-sequence normalization gives each sampled user total weight one; unnormalized exponential sums instead weight users by Z_n. Published RSS uses normalized exponential probabilities, samples targets with replacement, then removes selected targets from the input; this changes contexts, so it is not simply weighted causal next-item training. [Petrov and Macdonald, 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643).

Derived inclusion accounting: m independent draws give expected target multiplicity mp_t, but probability of appearing at least once is 1−(1−p_t)^m. Deduplicating draws therefore changes effective weights; averaging over a random number of unique targets introduces further normalization. For endpoint-sampled windows of L supervised targets, target t’s inclusion probability is Σ_e q(e)·1{e−L+1≤t≤e}. With window-mean loss, its expected coefficient is Σ_e q(e)·1{t∈W_e}/|W_e|. Thus exponential endpoint probabilities need not produce exponential target weights, especially near boundaries. Earlier targets excluded by fixed suffix truncation retain zero inclusion probability regardless of their loss weights.

Matching expected gradients does not match optimization trajectories. Sampling adds target-selection noise; deterministic summation removes that component conditional on the user and contexts. For objective Σ_t a_tℓ_t, sampling q_t requires gradient multiplier a_t/q_t; variance-minimizing probabilities are proportional to a_t‖∇ℓ_t‖, not necessarily recency. More draws change coverage and variance; summed versus averaged losses change scale, while additional optimizer steps change training exposure. [Zhao and Zhang, 2015](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/zhaoa15.pdf).
